s-Flame
Goals
• Use spherical diffusion flames in long-duration mg 
environment to: 
– obtain experimental data of exceptional quality in 
simple, well-defined flow fields.
– understand various key elemental diffusion flame 
processes.
• Compare these data with those obtained through 
independent computational simulation with detailed 
chemistry and transport in order to:
– scrutinize and improve the accuracy and 
comprehensiveness of these descriptions.

s-Flame Merits of One-Dimensional Flames 
for Fundamental Studies
• Flame structure fundamentally affected by 
aerodynamics.
• Simple flow and flame configuration facilitate 
experimentation, computation, analysis, and 
comparison, with enhanced accuracy and reliability.
• Reduced effort in describing flows allows more 
detailed study of other aspects of flames such as 
chemistry.
• A one-dimensional flame is the simplest possible 
configuration.

s-Flame
•
Only spherical (vs. planar and cylindrical) configuration admits 
steady-state 1D behavior in semi-infinite domain.
•
Spherically symmetric droplet combustion complicated by 
transient effects due to droplet heating and surface regression. 
Kinetics of large HC fuels also less well established.
•
Burner generation assures
steady-state surface boundary
conditions.
•
Planar flame in counterflow is not 1D
in terms of diffusion-convection as 
well as radiation misalignment.

s-Flame
I. Spreading of Diffusion Flame 
Sheets: Experimental
• Fuel/diluent mixtures will be issued from the spherical 
burner and ignited at flow rates expected to form flames that 
evolve toward idealized steady-state conditions
• As the flame spreads outward, transient measurements of 
flame-front velocity and flame structure will be obtained 
using imaging and radiometric systems
• The flame characteristics will be compared with the 
predictions of the transient numerical simulation of spherical 
diffusion flames for evaluations of detailed chemical 
kinetics and radiation models.

s-Flame
II. Flame Extinction: 
Experimental, Low Da
• Fuel/inert mixtures will be issued from the spherical burner and 
ignited at initial flow rates expected (or known/observed) to form 
flames that evolve toward idealized steady-state conditions
• Following ignition and initial flame front movement, the fuel/inert 
flow rate will be abruptly reduced to a second flow rate below the 
expected extinction limit
• Quasi-steady extinction is expected to occur as the flame adjusts to 
the reduced flow rate
• To refine the determination of the extinction flow rate for each 
fuel/diluent mixture, repeated tests are to be conducted at 
successively lower initial flow rates and higher secondary flow 
rates.

14
14
s-Flame
II. Flame Extinction: 
Experimental, High Da
• Fuel/inert mixtures will be issued from the spherical burner 
and ignited at flow rates slightly above and beyond that of 
the radiation extinction limit.
• Upon ignition the flame will grow and subsequently 
extinguish at the radiation extinction limit. 
• Rates of radiative emissions from the flame and radiative 
reabsorption elsewhere are to be accentuated in some cases 
by using a radiatively active diluent such as CO2.

15
15
s-Flame
III. Flamefront Instabilities: 
Phenomenology
• Stoichiometry constraint and lack of chemistry render 
diffusion flame sheets absolutely stable.
• However, chemistry becomes important for near-limit 
burning. Will flame become unstable? 
• Recent theories & experiments show instability 
characteristics similar to those of premixed flames for 
near-limit burning
• Since (positive) stretch suppresses cellular instability 
while promotes pulsating instability, the (stretchless) 
spherical flame is well suited for such studies.

16
16
s-Flame
III. Flamefront Instabilities:
Experimental
• Manipulate fuel and oxidizer Le through inert substitution
• Le<1: Cellularly unstable
• Le>1: Pulsatingly unstable
• Radiating diluents are used to further promote instability
• Pulsating instabilities are predicted
to occur near the extinction conditions
at both low and high Da, thereby
modifying the extinction mechanism
and limit; also allows for extinction 
detection and flame control

s-Flame
Fundamental Needs in Computational 
Aerothermochemistry
• Satisfactory quantitative description of 
combustion phenomena depends on: 
– Accurate input of physics & chemistry
– Computationally accessible
• Components of input:
– Turbulence (DNS & modeled)
– Chemistry (detailed & reduced)
– Diffusion (mixture & second order)
– Radiation (various models)

s-Flame
Complexities in 
Description of Chemistry
• Fuel oxidation is highly nonlinear and nonmonotonic in terms 
of temperature, pressure, and species concentrations
• Oxidation mechanisms consist of large number of species and 
reactions
• Characteristic reaction rates span over many orders of 
magnitude, hence computationally stiff
• Multicomponent diffusive transport can also be 
computationally expensive

s-Flame
Targets for Comprehensiveness in 
Experimental Data
• Broad coverage of thermodynamic states: temperature, 
pressure, concentration
• Ignition (homogeneous and diffusive): low-temperature 
chemistry
• Steady burning & extinction: high-temperature chemistry
• Premixed & diffusion flames: mixedness & time scale
• Global responses (flame speeds and extinction strain rates)
• Detailed flame structure (thermal and major/minor species)
• Pollutant chemistry

23
23
s-Flame The Role of mg Spherical Diffusion Flame in 
Comprehensive Mechanism Development
• Substantial research on homogeneous systems (shock 
tubes, flow reactors, etc.) and premixed flames
• Diffusion flame experiments mostly involve counter-
and stagnation flows, and droplet flames
• Burner-supported spherical flame is 1D and steady state
• Experiments of interest to chemistry are those involving 
ignition and extinction.
• Experiments for situations away from extinction would 
yield information on the diffusion and radiation 
parameters.

s-Flame
Development of Reduced Mechanisms
• Methodologies mostly in place for fast, systematic 
& accurate mechanism reduction
– Elimination of unimportant species & reactions
– Time-scale analysis (steady-state and partial equilibrium 
assumptions)
– Diffusion coefficient lumping
• Example: Detailed n-heptane mechanism with 561 
species and 2539 elementary reactions reduced to 
55 species and 51 lumped reactions

mg experimentation facilitates understanding of three

• Dual extinction limits: kinetic vs. radiation affected
• Flame-front instabilities and extinction monitoring

controlled mg experiments allow scrutiny and development of 
physical and chemical database, especially comprehensive 
detailed reaction mechanisms.

Experimental Approach  (2/6)
• Objective A – Flame Structure Evolution
–Fuel/diluent mixtures will be issued from the spherical 
burner and ignited at flow rates expected to form flames 
that evolve toward idealized steady-state conditions.
–As the flame spreads outward, transient measurements of 
flame front velocity and flame structure will be obtained 
using imaging and radiometric systems.  
–The flame characteristics will be compared with the 
predictions of the transient numerical simulation of 
spherical diffusion flames for evaluations of detailed 
chemical kinetic and transport models.

40
40
s-Flame
Experimental Approach  (3/6)
• Objective B – Quasi-Steady Extinction Limits, Low Da
–Fuel/inert mixtures will be issued from the spherical burner and 
ignited at initial flow rates expected (or known/observed) to 
form flames that evolve toward idealized steady-state conditions.  
–Following ignition and initial flame front movement, the 
fuel/inert flow rate will be abruptly reduced to a second flow 
rate below the expected extinction limit.  
–Quasi-steady extinction is expected to occur as the flame adjusts 
to the reduced flow rate.  
–To refine the determination of the extinction flow rate for each 
fuel/diluent mixture, repeated tests are to be conducted at 
successively lower initial flow rates and higher secondary flow 
rates.

41
41
s-Flame
Experimental Approach  (4/6)
• Objective B – Quasi-Steady Extinction Limits, Low Da
–At the low Da extinction limit, chemical kinetic rates are 
retarded with respect to flow rates by inert gas in the 
fuel stream that decreases the flame temperature.
–Based on theoretical predictions, fuel/inert mixtures are 
to be chosen for which the extinction flame radius is 
large enough to minimize the effects of heat loss to the 
burner.
–The surface temperature of the burner will be directly 
measured to quantify this loss.

42
42
s-Flame
Experimental Approach  (5/6)
• Objective B – Quasi-Steady Extinction Limits, High Da
–Fuel/inert mixtures will be issued from the spherical 
burner and ignited at flow rates above and beyond those 
expected (or known/observed) to form steady flames 
when radiative loss is considered.  
–The quasi-steady extinction is expected to occur as the 
flame moves outward before reaching the adiabatic
steady-state radius.
–Rates of radiative emissions from the flame and radiative 
reabsorption elsewhere are to be accentuated in some 
cases by using a radiatively active diluent such as CO2.

43
43
s-Flame
Experimental Approach  (6/6)
• Objective C – Flame Front Instabilities
–Pulsating flame front instabilities are predicted to occur 
near the extinction conditions at both low and high Da.
–The approach taken to observe the instabilities is similar to 
the approach for observing extinction except fuel/diluent 
mixtures with large system Lewis numbers (Le) are used.
• Low Da: moderate initial flow rate, abrupt change to flow rate 
below predicted extinction rate.
• High Da: initial flow rate above predicted extinction flow rate 
with radiation.
• Instabilities are expected to appear before extinction.
–Radiating diluents are used to further encourage the 
instabilities.
